summary: The board logic sits in one VHDL file (burnin_rubber.vhd) built as a raster-scan pipeline. 9-bit H/V counters drive the fetch phases for the foreground tiles, sprite attributes and background tiles. Sprites go through a 256x3 line buffer that is filled during the H-blank half of the line (hcnt(8)=1) and cleared as it is read, and priority and palette selection are decided per pixel. None of it follows MAME's screen_update_bnj / draw_chars / draw_sprites / draw_background decomposition or its per-frame bitmap compositing. The CPU memory map matches MAME, as any correct core must, and the opcode decryption is a simplified fixed bit swap, not MAME's DECO CPU-7 model.

findings.note: A 384-count hcnt and a vcnt run off a 6 MHz enable. The FG RAM address is muxed between the CPU, tile scan (vcnt_flip(7:3)&hcnt_flip(7:3)) and sprite-attribute scan (hcnt(6:2) when hcnt(8)=1), so the address comes from the counter bits. MAME's draw_chars instead loops offs over videoram and blits whole 8x8 tiles.

findings.signal: sprite line buffer filled during hblank
findings.note: Sprite attr/tile/Y bytes are latched at hcnt(3:0)=0/4/8 during the second half of the line. A vcnt+Y adder with an upper-nibble =="1111" check selects the visible row, pixels are written into a 3-bit line buffer whose start address is the sprite X, and the buffer is cleared on read-out. MAME loops over 8 sprites with transpen plus a wrap-around second draw.
A new sprite pixel overwrites the buffer unless it is 0, so priority is a read-modify-write on the line buffer, which is board-style logic. MAME gets the order implicitly from draw order.

fg_bits picks the sprite pixel when FG is transparent, or when the FG tile's low-priority bit (fg_grphx_addr(10)) is set and the sprite pixel is non-zero. The palette address then picks '1'&bg or '0'&fg per pixel. MAME instead does three passes: low-priority chars, then sprites, then high-priority chars over a copied bitmap.

findings.signal: background scrolled by adder on H counter
findings.note: The BG RAM address comes from bg_hcnt + {scroll1(1),scroll2} and vcnt bits, the tile ROM is fetched every 4 pixels, shift registers feed out the pixels, and a 4-stage skew pipeline aligns BG with FG. This is unlike MAME's pre-rendered 512-wide background bitmap and its scroll formula (scroll0&2)*128+511-scroll1.

findings.signal: BG enable as clear of shift registers
findings.note: With scroll1=0 the BG shift registers are held at zero, so the palette mux falls through to entry 8 per pixel. MAME takes a separate if/else branch in software.

The X/Y swap is a rewiring of the address lines (cpu_addr(4:0)&cpu_addr(9:5)) in one shared RAM, and the 'normal' half is the one oriented to the raster scan. MAME uses separate *_r/_w handlers that compute 32*y+x.

findings.signal: NMI latch cleared by write absent in MAME
findings.note: A coin edge sets a latched NMI that a CPU write to 0x1000 clears (raz_nmi_we). MAME's bnj_map has no write at 0x1000 and drives NMI directly from the port level.
Separate hsync0/hsync1/hsync2 waveforms are combined by a vsync line counter into csync with equalising pulses, which is monitor-side hardware detail that MAME does not model.

findings.signal: CPU memory map and I/O decode
findings.note: The address ranges and port order match MAME's maps, as any correct core must. The decode is written as comparisons on the top address bits.
The core swaps bits 5/6 on every SYNC fetch. MAME's DECO CPU-7 applies a bitswap only after a write. So the core diverges from MAME but does not clearly model the custom chip either.

The sound NMI is nmi_reg AND vcnt(3), which matches both the board and MAME's scanline&8. A discrete op-amp band-pass on AY2 channel A is simulated numerically, a circuit-level approach unlike MAME's device composition, but the derivation is visible only in comments.
